notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on Isaiah 14, drawn from the pages searched:

---

## VERSES 1–2: Mercy and Restoration for Israel

**v. 1: "For the LORD will have compassion on Jacob; once again He will choose Israel and settle them in their own land. The foreigner will join them and unite with the house of Jacob."**

The traditional reading sees this as a promise of return from Babylonian exile. God's destruction of Babylon (ch. 13) was driven by His purpose of mercy on Israel—Babylon had to fall so Israel could be restored (Pulpit Commentary). The phrase "once again He will choose Israel" means that the exile was a kind of rejection; the restoration is a fresh, gracious election, not something Israel had any claim to (Pulpit). David Guzik adds a pastoral point: sometimes believers feel that if God had to choose again, He would not choose them—but here God says He *would* choose Israel all over again (Enduring Word). Gill notes that "strangers" refers to proselytes who would join Israel and cleave to them, with partial fulfillment at the return from Babylon and fuller fulfillment in the gospel age when Gentiles joined believing Jews (Gill). Ellicott traces successive fulfillments: Persian support for the returning exiles, proselytes in the apostolic age (Acts 2:10; 6:5), and finally the admission of Gentiles into the kingdom of Christ (Ellicott).

**v. 2: "The nations will escort Israel… Then the house of Israel will possess the nations as menservants and maidservants… They will make captives of their captors and rule over their oppressors."**

The "people" (literally "peoples") bringing Israel home points to the edict of Cyrus and the support given by neighbours (Ezra 1:4, 6). Gill notes that some think this was fulfilled in Maccabean times, but more fully in the spiritual sense through the spread of the gospel by Jewish apostles, by which many nations were brought under the obedience of Christ (Gill). Ellicott says no period of later Jewish history has literally seen the people ruling over a conquered race—the true fulfilment has been in the triumph of Israel's leading ideas and the victory of the faith of Christ (Ellicott). Guzik takes the reversal of captors/captives as a picture of how the ultimate way to conquer an enemy is to make them your friend—Gentiles are brought in and become servants in the Lord's land (Enduring Word).

---

## VERSES 3–8: Rest from Bondage and the Taunt Song Begins

**v. 3: "On the day that the LORD gives you rest from your pain and torment, and from the hard labor into which you were forced…"**

The condition of the exiles in Babylon is described in nearly the same terms as in Habakkuk 2:13. Ellicott notes that a monarch bent on building projects who had carried off all the skilled labour of Jerusalem was likely to vex them with "fear" and "hard bondage"—as Assurbanipal boasted of making Arabian prisoners carry heavy burdens and build brick-work (Ellicott). Gill notes that the hard bondage in Babylon, though not detailed like the Egyptian bondage, included sorrow at being away from the land and the free exercise of religion (Gill). Guzik applies this devotionally: rest from sorrow, fear, and hard bondage is the birthright of every believer in Jesus Christ, who said "Come to Me… and I will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28) (Enduring Word).

**v. 4: "you will sing this song of contempt against the king of Babylon: How the oppressor has ceased, and how his fury has ended!"**

The word translated "proverb" (*mashal*) here means a taunting speech or derisive song (Ellicott, Pulpit). The Pulpit Commentary notes the LXX renders it "lamentation"—yet it is mock-lament, a funeral dirge that really mocks. Guzik notes the literary form: the "limping rhythm of a Hebrew lament" is used ironically—this is a taunt in the guise of a lament, for a king who receives no burial (Enduring Word). "The golden city ceased"—there is debate about the Hebrew word *madhebah*. Ellicott notes the general consensus of recent critics follows the Targum and LXX for "task-master" or "place of torture," though the Vulgate renders "how has the tribute ceased" (Ellicott). The Pulpit Commentary prefers "golden," from the Chaldee *d'hab* (gold), matching Babylon's reputation for gold (Pulpit).

**v. 5: "The LORD has broken the staff of the wicked, the scepter of the rulers."**

The "staff" and "scepter" are symbols of power—the staff being what one leans on, the scepter what one wields to smite (Ellicott). Gill notes that though the Lord used Cyrus as His instrument, the work was His own: He broke the power of the wicked kings of Babylon (Gill). The breaking signifies utter destruction and cessation of authority.

**v. 6: "It struck the peoples in anger with unceasing blows; it subdued the nations in rage with relentless persecution."**

Ellicott translates: "a stroke without ceasing" and "a trampling that is not stayed" (Ellicott). The verse describes the relentless military aggression of Babylon—one war following another without pause (Pulpit). Gill notes that even those spared were ruled with rigour and oppressive tribute (Gill).

**v. 7: "All the earth is at peace and at rest; they break out in song."**

Ellicott observes that the phrase "break forth into singing" is characteristic of Isaiah (also 44:23; 49:13; 52:9; 54:1; 55:12) and not found elsewhere—the emancipated nations exult in unfamiliar peace (Ellicott). The Pulpit Commentary notes there was historically an interval of about eleven years between Cyrus's conquest of Babylon (538 BC) and Cambyses's expedition against Egypt (527 BC) (Pulpit).

**v. 8: "Even the cypresses and cedars of Lebanon exult over you: 'Since you have been laid low, no woodcutter comes against us.'"**

There is a double meaning. Literally: the Assyrian and Babylonian kings cut timber extensively in Lebanon for building projects; the Persians did not, so the forests were spared (Pulpit, Ellicott). Metaphorically: trees represent kings and nobles (cf. Ezekiel 31:16) who also had respite (Pulpit). Guzik adds that the trees also rejoice at the fall of the spiritual king of Babylon because creation itself will be delivered from the bondage of corruption (Romans 8:21) (Enduring Word). Gill notes a similar metaphorical sense: the "fir trees" and "cedars" represent rulers and the rich who are no longer in fear (Gill).

---

## VERSES 9–11: Sheol Receives the King

**v. 9: "Sheol beneath is eager to meet you upon your arrival. It stirs the spirits of the dead to greet you—all the rulers of the earth. It makes all the kings of the nations rise from their thrones."**

Sheol is the shadow-world, the region of the dead (Ellicott). The Pulpit Commentary describes it as a dismal region in the centre of the earth where departed souls descended; personal identity and continued consciousness after death are assumed (Pulpit). The "dead" (*Rephaim*) are the "feeble ones"—shades regarded as weak compared to living men, like Homer's *eidōla kamontōn* (Pulpit, Ellicott). Ellicott notes the "chief ones" are literally "he-goats" or bell-wethers of the flock (Ellicott). Guzik says "Hell itself is excited to meet the king of Babylon because it can't wait to be the place where the one who tortured so many is tortured himself"—true for both the literal and spiritual king (Enduring Word). The kings rise from their thrones: in Sheol, former earthly rank seems recognized and maintained (Pulpit).

**v. 10: "They will all respond to you, saying, 'You too have become weak, as we are; you have become like us!'"**

The question implies an affirmative answer—the king of Babylon is found as weak as the shadowy forms of the dead (Ellicott). Gill: the one who was looked upon as invincible, even immortal, even a deity, is now "sick" (the Hebrew word), brought to death, stripped of all natural strength and civil power (Gill).

**v. 11: "Your pomp has been brought down to Sheol, along with the music of your harps. Maggots are your bed and worms your blanket."**

The Pulpit Commentary notes that the Babylonians were fond of music and had many instruments (Daniel 3:7, 10); now all kingly state moulders in the grave, with maggots and worms replacing costly shawls and carpets on which the great king once rested (Ellicott, Pulpit). Guzik applies this to the spiritual king: Satan was associated with music in heaven, based on Ezekiel 28:13, and the sound of his stringed instruments is only brought down when he is imprisoned in hell (Enduring Word).

---

## VERSES 12–15: The Fall of the Day Star (Lucifer)

**This is the most debated passage in the chapter. The central dispute is whether these verses refer (a) only to the human king of Babylon, (b) only to Satan, or (c) to both in a dual fulfillment.**

**v. 12: "How you have fallen from heaven, O day star, son of the dawn! You have been cut down to the ground, O destroyer of nations."**

The Hebrew word is *helel* ("shining one"), referring to the planet Venus as the morning star. "Lucifer" is from the Latin Vulgate (*lucifer* = light-bearer), etymologically equivalent to the Greek *phōsphoros* (Ellicott). The Pulpit Commentary says Babylon's sudden fall is compared to the seeming fall of a star from heaven (Pulpit). Ellicott notes that while "Lucifer" became a medieval Latin name for Satan, "few English readers realise the fact that it is the king of Babylon, and not the devil, who is addressed as Lucifer," and that the "morning star" has risen to become a name of Christ (Revelation 22:16) (Ellicott).

**The different traditions on vv. 12–15:**

- **John Calvin (Reformed):** Explicitly rejected any reference to Satan. "The exposition of this passage, which some have given, as if it referred to Satan, has arisen from ignorance; for the context plainly shows that these statements must be understood in reference to the king of the Babylonians.… But as these inventions have no probability whatever, let us pass by them as useless fables" (Enduring Word, quoting Calvin).

- **Adam Clarke (Methodist/Wesleyan):** Also rejected the Satan interpretation: "the text speaks nothing at all concerning Satan nor his fall, nor the occasion of that fall… This chapter speaks not of the ambition and fall of Satan, but of the pride, arrogance, and fall of Nebuchadnezzar" (Enduring Word, quoting Clarke).

- **David Guzik / Enduring Word (Charismatic/Pentecostal):** Strongly advocates a dual fulfillment. "In the prophetic habit of speaking to both a near and a distant fulfillment, the prophet will sometimes speak more to the near or more to the distant… There was a far more brightly shining being who inhabited heaven and fell even more dramatically—the king of spiritual Babylon, Satan." He outlines four falls of Satan: (1) from glorified to profane (Ezekiel 28:14-16; Luke 10:18); (2) from access to heaven to restriction on earth (Revelation 12:9); (3) from earth to the bottomless pit (Revelation 20:1-3); (4) from the pit to the lake of fire (Revelation 20:10)—this passage referring to the final, fourth fall (Enduring Word).

- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** "Though the words are addressed to the fallen king of Babylon, it is evident that its ultimate thrust is at Satan himself, by whom the king was manipulated into rebellion against the Most High" (StudyLight.org).

- **Ligonier (Reformed):** "It is clear that this text is not speaking directly of the devil… Even though a specific king is not mentioned, the prophet still has a human ruler in view (vv. 3–4), so Isaiah was not talking about the Enemy when he gave this prophecy. Nevertheless, we will not be too hard on church history. Even we might draw an indirect analogy between the fall of the prideful ruler of Babylon and the fall of Satan from grace" (Ligonier, search excerpt).

- **John Piper / Desiring God (Reformed Baptist):** Discusses Satan's fall and the origin of evil, sees Satan as a created holy angel who rebelled, and connects the sin to self-exaltation, but also acknowledges mystery about *how* the first sinful inclination arose (Desiring God, search excerpt).

- **NET Bible (modern scholarship):** "The primary or initial reference of 'morning star' is not to the devil but to the Babylonian king.… At the same time, Isa 14:12–15 seems to go beyond a description of a mortal king. Further, if Jesus in Luke 10:18 and John in Rev 9:1 had this passage in mind, then it is evident that there is a secondary meaning that relates to the devil himself. A double-fulfillment prophecy is thus probably in view" (bible.org, quoting NET Bible footnote).

- **bible.org article:** Notes that the KJV "Lucifer" argument against modern translations is weak; the Hebrew *helel* simply means "shining one" or "morning star." The footnote in NET Bible says the whole section (vv. 4b-21) is directed to the king of Babylon, "who is clearly depicted as a human ruler. Other kings of the earth address him in vv. 9ff., he is called 'the man' in v. 16, and, according to vv. 19-20, he possesses a physical body" (bible.org).

**v. 13: "You said in your heart: 'I will ascend to the heavens; I will raise my throne above the stars of God. I will sit on the mount of assembly, in the far reaches of the north.'"**

Ellicott explains that the boast represents an apotheosis—a self-deification. The Babylonian kings claimed divine-like status (Shalmaneser described himself as "a sun-god," Assurbanipal as "lord of all kings") (Ellicott). The "mount of assembly" is now understood by most modern scholars not as Mount Zion but as the mythical mountain of Babylonian theosophy where the gods sat in council—the Babylonians had a mountain called *Im-Kharsak* or *Kharsak-Kurra*, "the mighty mountain of Bel, whose head rivals heaven, whose root is the holy deep," regarded as where the ark rested and the gods had their seat (Pulpit). "The far reaches of the north" reflects ancient Near Eastern geography where the divine mountain was thought to be in the farthest north, akin to the Greek Hyperborei legend or Indian Meru (Ellicott). The Pulpit Commentary identifies this with Mount Elwend near Ecbatana or the peak of Rowandiz, both northeast of Babylon—a position described as "north" in ancient idiom (Pulpit).

**v. 14: "I will ascend above the tops of the clouds; I will make myself like the Most High."**

The title "Most High" (*Elyon*) was not exclusively Israelite but common to Phoenicians and other kindred nations (Genesis 14:18) (Ellicott). The Pulpit Commentary notes that the Assyrian and Babylonian kings never actually assumed the divine title "god," unlike Egyptian pharaohs; Isaiah is representing the *inner thought* of the monarch—he acted as though he were a god, wrapped up in himself, not bowing to any higher Power (Pulpit). Guzik sees the five "I will" statements as the essence of the self-obsessed life: not so much a desire to be above God as to be exalted above one's peers—to be the highest among all creatures (Enduring Word).

**v. 15: "But you will be brought down to Sheol, to the lowest depths of the Pit."**

The indignant sarcasm is noted: the proud king sought the "recesses" (*yarketê*) of the divine mountain in the north; instead he finds the "recesses" of the pit—the lowest parts of Sheol (Ellicott, Pulpit). For those who see a Satanic reference, this is the final fall to the lake of fire (Enduring Word).

---

## VERSES 16–21: The Corpse of the Tyrant

**v. 16: "Those who see you will stare; they will ponder your fate: 'Is this the man who shook the earth and made the kingdoms tremble…'"**

The scene shifts back to earth. The corpse of the mighty conqueror lies unburied on the battlefield, and onlookers scarcely believe their eyes—they must look closely to confirm it is indeed the great king (Pulpit, Ellicott). Guzik notes the same will happen when the spiritual king falls: people will see him for what he really is and be amazed at how much power he actually had (Enduring Word).

**v. 17: "who turned the world into a desert and destroyed its cities, who refused to let the captives return to their homes?"**

Ellicott observes this was a characteristic feature of Assyrian cruelty: Sennacherib and Assurbanipal boast of having carried off captive kings in "chains of iron" and keeping them chained like dogs in the palace court. Jehoiachin was imprisoned for thirty-seven years (Jeremiah 52:31) (Ellicott). The Pulpit Commentary suggests it is the retention of the entire Jewish people in captivity that is foremost in the prophet's mind (Pulpit).

**v. 18: "All the kings of the nations lie in state, each in his own tomb."**

The "house" in which the monarchs lie is their sepulchre, often almost literally the "house" or palace of the dead, as with Egyptian pyramid graves (Ellicott). The contrast is being set up: even pagan kings receive honourable burial.

**v. 19: "But you are cast out of your grave like a rejected branch, covered by those slain with the sword, and dumped into a rocky pit like a carcass trampled underfoot."**

Guzik notes: "even the common man regarded proper burial as essential"—but the king of Babylon gets a bed of maggots and a blanket of worms instead (Enduring Word). The "abominable branch" (*neser*) is a scion that is mildewed and blasted, flung away as loathsome—a sharp contrast to the righteous Branch from the stump of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1) (Ellicott, Enduring Word). Ellicott adds that to lie unburied, "a prey to dogs and vultures" (Homer, *Iliad* i.4), was the shame of all shames in the ancient world (Ellicott).

**v. 20: "You will not join them in burial, since you have destroyed your land and slaughtered your own people. The offspring of the wicked will never again be mentioned."**

The curse of dishonoured death is connected with its cause: the conqueror had inflicted that shame even on his own people and was punished in like kind (Ellicott). Jeremiah's prediction about Jehoiakim (Jeremiah 22:19) and parallel instances in 2 Chronicles 21:20; 24:25 are noted (Ellicott). The phrase "shall never be named" means the dynasty would be blotted out—historically, the dynasty of Nabopolassar disappeared, and Darius boasted of subduing an impostor claiming to represent it (Ellicott, citing the Behistun inscription).

**v. 21: "Prepare a place to slaughter his sons for the iniquities of their forefathers. They will never rise up to possess a land or cover the earth with their cities."**

The command may be addressed to the Medes (Isaiah 13:17) or any minister of divine vengeance (Ellicott). Ellicott notes that in the judgment of God as seen in history, judgment falls on the last members of an evil dynasty—in this sense the sins of the fathers are visited on the children—while in the eternal judgment behind the veil, each soul stands on its own responsibility (Ezekiel 18:4) (Ellicott). Gill notes that Belshazzar had "wives and concubines" (Daniel 5:2) and therefore probably children; Cyrus may have spared them, but Cambyses or Darius would likely have put them to death when Babylon threatened revolt (Pulpit / Gill).

---

## VERSES 22–23: Babylon Wiped Out

**v. 22: "'I will rise up against them,' declares the LORD of Hosts. 'I will cut off from Babylon her name and her remnant, her offspring and her posterity,' declares the LORD."**

These verses form the epilogue of the taunt-song, making clear that the punishment comes from Jehovah, whose Name appears twice in v. 22 and emphatically closes v. 23 (Pulpit). Ellicott notes that "name" here likely means "fame" or "celebrity" (Deuteronomy 26:19; Zephaniah 3:20). "Son and nephew" is literally "son and grandson"—every word for descent is heaped together for emphasis (Ellicott). Guzik sees this as true of both literal and spiritual Babylon: there will not even be a remnant left (Enduring Word).

**v. 23: "'I will make her a place for owls and for swamplands; I will sweep her away with the broom of destruction,' declares the LORD of Hosts."**

The Pulpit Commentary notes the swampy character of the country around Babylon's ruins arises from neglect of the dams along the Euphrates (Pulpit). The creature translated "bittern" or "owl" or "porcupine" is uncertain; the LXX and Vulgate give "hedgehog," but since it is associated with pools of water, some kind of waterfowl (like the bittern, *Botaurus stellaris*) is preferred (Ellicott). "I will sweep it with the broom of destruction": Babylon is swept away as one sweeps foul rubbish from a house—the world is cleaner for its destruction (Ellicott). Guzik quotes Spurgeon: "If God's enemies have a bright day or two, it shall soon be showery weather with them. They may for the moment exult over God's people, but he knows that their day of reckoning is coming" (Enduring Word).

---

## VERSES 24–27: God's Purpose against Assyria

**v. 24: "The LORD of Hosts has sworn: 'Surely, as I have planned, so will it be; as I have purposed, so will it stand.'"**

From the distant prospect of deliverance from Babylon, the prophet turns to a nearer enemy: Assyria (Pulpit). The key word is "sworn"—God seldom confirms His purposes with an oath, doing so only in condescension to human weakness (Hebrews 6:17), to give the assurance people refuse to give to a bare assertion (Pulpit). Gill notes that all that was prophesied about Babylon's destruction was "settled and fixed by the purpose of God, which could not be made void" (Gill).

**v. 25: "I will break Assyria in My land; I will trample him on My mountain. His yoke will be taken off My people, and his burden removed from their shoulders."**

This found fulfillment in the destruction of Sennacherib's army. The "mountains" are the hills round Jerusalem where the Assyrian army was encamped; they are sacred as "my mountains" (Ellicott). The Pulpit Commentary notes this may refer to the disaster to Sargon's forces or Sennacherib's (Pulpit). The Assyrian yoke, imposed by Tiglath-Pileser (2 Kings 16:7-10) and again by Sargon, was thrown off by Hezekiah (Pulpit).

**v. 26: "This is the plan devised for the whole earth, and this is the hand stretched out over all the nations."**

The fall of Assyria and Babylon does not stand alone but forms part of a scheme embracing all nations and all ages (Ellicott, referencing Isaiah 9:12). The judgment on Assyria is a paradigm of God's universal judgment.

**v. 27: "The LORD of Hosts has purposed, and who can thwart Him? His hand is outstretched, so who can turn it back?"**

Ellicott renders more emphatically: "His is the outstretched hand" (Ellicott). Precept Austin notes: "God Himself has taken an OATH and swears that these events will happen exactly as God has intended and will turn out exactly as He has planned. God's sovereign purposes regarding Assyria and Babylon will be carried out" (Precept Austin).

---

## VERSES 28–32: Warning to Philistia

**v. 28: "In the year that King Ahaz died, this burden was received."**

The death-year of Ahaz was 727 BC. Ellicott notes it was natural that the prophet's thoughts should be much exercised then, as in the year of Uzziah's death (Isaiah 6:1), on the uncertainties of the coming future. The "burden" was the answer to his searchings of heart, probably delivered before the king's death (Ellicott).

**v. 29: "Do not rejoice, all you Philistines, that the rod that struck you is broken. For a viper will spring from the root of the snake, and a flying serpent from its egg."**

The Philistines were rejoicing at the death of a king of Judah (possibly Ahaz, or an Assyrian oppressor whose death they thought spelled relief). But the prophet warns: a worse oppressor is coming. The imagery of the viper springing from the root of the snake means the successor will be more dangerous than the predecessor (Pulpit). Gill interprets the "rod" as the Assyrian king who had oppressed Philistia; his death brought no true relief (Gill).

**v. 30: "Then the firstborn of the poor will find pasture, and the needy will lie down in safety, but I will kill your root by famine, and your remnant will be slain."**

While Philistia is destroyed, God's afflicted people in Judah will find provision and safety. The "firstborn of the poor" is a poetic way of saying "the poorest of the poor"—those most vulnerable—will be cared for. The contrast is stark: Philistia's root perishes; the poor of God's people flourish.

**v. 31: "Wail, O gate! Cry out, O city! Melt away, all you Philistines! For a cloud of smoke comes from the north, and there are no stragglers in its ranks."**

The "cloud of smoke from the north" is an invading army—the Assyrian forces coming down the coastal plain. There are "no stragglers"—the army is disciplined, relentless, and unstoppable.

**v. 32: "What answer will be given to the envoys of that nation? 'The LORD has founded Zion, where His afflicted people will find refuge.'"**

Ellicott: "This is the answer to all such inquiries. Zion stands firm and safe in the protection of Jehovah. The 'poor'… shall find refuge in it. They need no foreign alliances, no arm of flesh" (Ellicott). The Pulpit Commentary adds that Zion is of the Lord's founding and under His care and protection; His people have great reason to trust in Him (Pulpit). Precept Austin notes that "the poor in spirit find refuge in Zion because God's place of security is not for the self-sufficient but for those who recognize their need for Him" (Precept Austin).

---

## Summary of Key Disputed Points

**The identity of "Lucifer" / "Day Star" in vv. 12–15:**

| Tradition | Position | Key Source |
|---|---|---|
| John Calvin (Reformed) | Human king of Babylon only; Satan reference is "ignorance" and "useless fables" | Enduring Word (quoting Calvin) |
| Adam Clarke (Methodist) | Human king only; text says nothing about Satan's fall | Enduring Word (quoting Clarke) |
| Ligonier (Reformed) | Not directly about Satan, but indirect analogy is permissible | ligonier.org |
| John MacArthur / GTY (Baptist) | Dual reference: king of Babylon and Satan who energized him | Precept Austin (quoting MacArthur Study Bible) |
| David Guzik / Enduring Word (Charismatic) | Dual fulfillment; primarily about Satan's final fall | enduringword.com |
| Garner-Howes (Baptist) | Ultimate thrust is at Satan behind the human king | studylight.org |
| NET Bible (scholarly) | Primary: human king. Secondary: Satan, given NT usage (Luke 10:18) | bible.org |
| John Piper / Desiring God (Reformed Baptist) | Connects to Satan's fall and origin of evil; acknowledges mystery | desiringgod.org |
